lead: Moment distribution finds support moments of a continuous beam one joint at a time. Lock every joint, write fixed end moments, then unlock a joint: its unbalanced moment is shared by member stiffness, and half of each share is carried to a fixed far end. It checks computer results and shows how stiffness pulls moment toward the stiffer member.
prereq: You need statically indeterminate beams for compatibility, Clapeyron’s three-moment equation for a second route, and fixed end moments of single spans.

sections.h3: The idea and the sign convention

blocks.text: A continuous beam has more unknown support moments than equilibrium equations. The three-moment equation solves them together; moment distribution solves them one joint at a time. Imagine every internal joint is locked against rotation; simple supports remain pins. The loads produce fixed end moments (FEM) at member ends. These generally do not balance at a joint. Unlock the joint; it rotates until the moments at the joint sum to zero. The rotation spreads moment into the connected members. Re-lock the joint and move to the next joint. Repeat until carry-over is small. Use one sign convention: clockwise moments on member ends are positive. Hogging at both ends gives opposite signs, and sagging at both ends also gives opposite signs. Hogging at one end and sagging at the other give the same sign. Write the sign beside every FEM. The method is also called the Hardy Cross method.

Member stiffness k is the moment at one end needed to rotate that end by one radian. For length L and flexural rigidity EI: k = 4EI/L with the far end fixed; k = 3EI/L with the far end pinned (held in position, free to rotate). At a joint, DF<sub>i</sub> = k<sub>i</sub> / Σk, where Σk is the sum of member stiffnesses there. Distribution factors at one joint sum to 1. A stiffer member takes a larger share. The propped cantilever FEM is wL²/8 at the fixed end for uniform load w over span L, and 3PL/16 for a central point load. The carry-over factor is ½ for a fixed far end and 0 for a pinned far end. Never carry over to a pinned end. Carry-over is why one pass may not be enough: a moment carried to a fixed end changes the balance there.

items: Columns at each joint: member, relative stiffness, DF, FEM, balance, carry over, final moment.
k = 4EI/L with far end fixed, 3EI/L with far end pinned.
DF = k/Σk at each joint; factors sum to 1.
Write each FEM with its sign.
Unbalanced U = sum of FEMs; apply balancing moment −U split by DF.
Carry over ½ of each balance to a fixed far end; carry 0 to a pinned end.
Repeat at other joints until carry-over is small.
Add all contributions at each end for the final moment.
Check: final moments at each joint sum to zero.

figure.caption: Worked example 2: the same two spans with A fixed. At B the fixed-far-end span BA (k = 4EI/6) and the pinned-far-end span BC (k = 3EI/4) share the 10 kN·m unbalance as 0.471 and 0.529. Half of BA’s share is carried to A; nothing goes to the pin at C. The final moments are 32.35 kN·m at A and 25.29 kN·m at B, both hogging.

spec.aria: A two-span beam fixed in a wall at A, on a pin at B 6 metres along and a roller at C 4 metres further, under 10 kilonewtons per metre. Below, a moment distribution table with columns AB, BA and BC: stiffness 0.667 and 0.75, distribution factors 0, 0.471 and 0.529, fixed end moments minus 30, plus 30 and minus 20, balance minus 4.71 and minus 5.29, a carry-over of minus 2.35 to AB shown by an arrow, and final moments minus 32.35, plus 25.29 and minus 25.29.

examples.question: A continuous beam has spans AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, a uniform load w = 10 kN/m on both spans, simple supports at A and C, and continuity at B. Find the bending moment at B by moment distribution.
steps: Both far ends pinned, so k = 3EI/L: k<sub>BA</sub> = 0.5EI/m, k<sub>BC</sub> = 0.75EI/m, Σk = 1.25EI/m; DF<sub>BA</sub> = 0.40, DF<sub>BC</sub> = 0.60.
FEM = wL²/8: FEM<sub>BA</sub> = 10×6²/8 = +45 kN·m; FEM<sub>BC</sub> = −10×4²/8 = −20 kN·m.
Shares: −25×0.40 = −10 kN·m on BA; −25×0.60 = −15 kN·m on BC. Carry-over = 0 because both far ends are pinned.
Final: M<sub>BA</sub> = +45 −10 = +35 kN·m; M<sub>BC</sub> = −20 −15 = −35 kN·m. Check: +35 −35 = 0.
examples.answer: The moment at B is 35 kN·m hogging, the same as the three-moment equation gives.
examples.check:
w, L1, L2 = 10, 6, 4
kBA, kBC = 3/L1, 3/L2
S = kBA + kBC
DFBA, DFBC = kBA/S, kBC/S
FEMBA, FEMBC = w*L1**2/8, -w*L2**2/8
U = FEMBA + FEMBC
bal = -U
MBA = FEMBA + bal*DFBA
MBC = FEMBC + bal*DFBC
for x in (kBA, kBC, DFBA, DFBC, FEMBA, FEMBC, U, bal, bal*DFBA, bal*DFBC, MBA, MBC):
    print(f'{x:g}')

examples.question: Change the beam of worked example 1 so that A is fixed; C stays a simple support. Spans 6 m and 4 m, w = 10 kN/m on both, constant EI. Find the support moments by moment distribution and check them with the three-moment equation.
steps: Stiffness at B: BA has a fixed far end, k = 4EI/6 = 0.667EI/m; BC has a pinned far end, k = 3EI/4 = 0.75EI/m. Σk = 1.417EI/m. DF<sub>BA</sub> = 0.471, DF<sub>BC</sub> = 0.529.
Fixed end moments: AB fixed both ends, FEM<sub>AB</sub> = −wL²/12 = −30 kN·m, FEM<sub>BA</sub> = +30 kN·m; BC with C pinned, FEM<sub>BC</sub> = −wL²/8 = −20 kN·m.
Joint B: unbalanced +30 − 20 = +10 kN·m. Balance −10: BA gets −4.71, BC gets −5.29 kN·m.
Carry-over: half of −4.71 goes to A, −2.35 kN·m. Nothing goes to C (pinned). A is fixed, so it is never released; one cycle finishes the job.
Final: M<sub>AB</sub> = −30 − 2.35 = −32.35 kN·m; M<sub>BA</sub> = 30 − 4.71 = +25.29; M<sub>BC</sub> = −20 − 5.29 = −25.29. Joint B sums to zero.

Check by three moments with a zero-length span beyond A: 12M<sub>A</sub> + 6M<sub>B</sub> = −540 and 6M<sub>A</sub> + 20M<sub>B</sub> = −700 give M<sub>A</sub> = −32.35 and M<sub>B</sub> = −25.29 kN·m (hogging).
examples.answer: Hogging moments 32.35 kN·m at the fixed end A and 25.29 kN·m at B. Fixing A pulls moment towards A and lowers the moment at B from 35 to 25.29 kN·m.

traps: DFs not summing to 1. Recompute DF = k/Σk.
Using 4EI/L when the far end is pinned. Use 3EI/L and carry-over 0.
Carrying over to a pinned end, or forgetting the ½ carry-over to a fixed end.
Mixing sign conventions. Fix clockwise positive on member ends and keep it.
Wrong sign on the balancing moment. U = sum of FEMs; apply −U.

quiz.q: What is the distribution factor at a joint?
quiz.a: DF<sub>i</sub> = k<sub>i</sub>/Σk, where Σk is the sum of member stiffnesses at the joint; the factors sum to 1.

quiz.q: Give the carry-over factor for a fixed far end and a pinned far end.
Why is a member with a pinned far end less stiff than one with a fixed far end?
quiz.a: The pinned end rotates freely, so less moment rotates the near end by one radian; k is 3EI/L not 4EI/L.

quiz.q: Two members meet at a joint with k = 2EI and k = 3EI. Find their distribution factors.
At a joint the FEMs are +30 and −10 kN·m. The distribution factors are 0.25 and 0.75. Find the balancing shares.
quiz.a: U = +20 kN·m; balancing moment = −20 kN·m; shares = −5 and −15 kN·m.

quiz.q: Why does moment distribution converge faster when the far ends are pinned?
quiz.a: Carry-over is 0, so balancing one joint does not disturb the far joint; fixed ends carry ½ onward and need more cycles.

quiz.q: In worked example 2, find the vertical reaction at the fixed end A.
quiz.a: Span AB as a free body with hogging end moments 32.35 at A and 25.29 at B: R<sub>A</sub> = wL/2 + (32.35 − 25.29)/6 = 30 + 1.18 = 31.18 kN.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hardy Cross published the method in the 1930s, when frame analysis was done by hand. It stayed standard for continuous beams until the stiffness matrix and computers took over. Modern software assembles the same stiffness values and solves all joints at once. The method still gives a quick check and shows which member attracts moment.
